chapters.title: Seattle & Olympic National Park
chapters.text:
Day one of the bikepacking adventure.  We took a ferry from Seattle across Puget Sound to the peninsula and out to Mount Olympus National Park.   One night camped next to Puget Sound, one night at Lake Crescent.  

Leaving Lake Crescent, we had our first experience riding single track through the beautiful temperate rainforests of the Pacific North-West where tragedy struck.  Ross's pedal hit a rock and brought his bike to a sudden stop while he continued to soar, over the handlebars and directly into the ground.  He suffered a critical strike to his shoulder, snapping his collar bone in twain.  Thus altering our plans.  

The rescue operation took us the rest of the day as we walked out of the forest and went knocking on doors for help.  A kind local whisked him away to the nearest hospital for an assessment while I doubled back to retrieve my bike and finished the trail to reunite with him.  From there we bussed back to Poulsbo and took refuge in a motel.  

The following day, Ross' cousins traveled from Portland to collect him and take him under their care.  The remainder of our three month bikepacking adventure was now mine to do solo.

photos.desc: Thank you to the Griswolds for hosting me for a night in their treehouse.  Amazing.

chapters.title: North Bend
chapters.text:
Riding from Seattle to North Bend was a treat.  Campuses set in forests.  Bridges hopping from island to island.  Tree lined trails.  Also highways.  I learned a lesson about just letting RideWithGPS curate your journey.  I probably should have trusted my senses better and not just followed it blindly.  It took me down into a valley and up a near vertical climb, carrying my bike for parts.  It spat me out, sweaty and covered in debris at some kind of sterile golf village that looked like it was out of Edward Scissorhands.

Anyway, I made it to North Bend and stayed with a kind family who let me sleep in their treehouse for a couple of nights.  North Bend is where a lot of Twin Peaks was filmed, in particular the scenes in the opening sequence and the diner.  Wholesome vibes, I can see why Agent Cooper fell in love with the place.  I stayed two nights here, spending a day just exploring the town, swimming in the river and washing my clothes.  Good times.

photos.desc: "Diane, a small town is not unlike a river—lots of hidden currents and eddies, each holding its own secret... If you ever find yourself in this neck of the woods, you must come here. It's a place where a step off the road means a step into the wild." - Dale Cooper
The famous scene from the intro of Twin Peaks

I came across a guy resting on a log in the river bed, reading a book, with his Bengal cat exploring freely around him.  Said once he chased it down over 10 miles with an air tracker that it wears after it got lost.  Wild.
Coffee, black as midnight on a moonless night.
Thank you Del C. for putting me up for a couple of nights in his majestic treehouse.  That was two different treehouses over two nights.  How lucky!

chapters.title: John Wayne Trail, Snoqualmie Pass, Ellensburg
chapters.text:
The Palouse to Cascades State Park Trail aka John Wayne Pioneer Trail aka Iron Horse Trail, is an old railroad track converted into biking trail, running from North Bend all the way across the state of Washington to the Washington / Idaho border.  

I jumped on it at the start at Rattlesnake Lake, near North Bend.  Old rail lines make great bike trails.  The grades are consistently low and easy to ride, and they take you through some fantastic landscapes.

Washington state consists of two parts.  The temperate, cool and wet rainforested side of the Cascade Mountains.  And the other side which is like Mars.  Dry and hot as f*ck (though I think Mars is cold?).  Once you pass over the Cascade Mountains it becomes a dustbowl.  It's astonishing.  This segment of the journey was lovely.  I passed through a long railroad tunnel in total darkness but for my torch.  Camped in a rainforest.  Passed through some charming old school cowboy towns.  Camping at Cle Elum Lake was something.  Some redneck woke us all up at 6am as he ripped open the engine of his boat at a dam which acted as a loudspeaker.  What hell he unleashed.  

I spent another night next to the Yakima river and shared the site with 3 other bike packers from Seattle.  Legends whose names I can't remember.  But they lent me a can opener which I was still lacking, and they shared their booze with me.  Good company!

Descending from the Cascade Mountains I got to Ellensberg.  I'd only heard of it before as the home of singer Mark Lanegan.  He didn't have nice things to say about it.  But he didn't have nice things to say about anything.  I thought it was charming.  Hot as f.  But the architecture was nice.  There was a bit of hipster cool here and there but mostly it's a hub for a farming community.  I was put up for a night by a couple who gave me a nice feed and a warm bed.  Greatly appreciated!  He had spent some time living in Buenos Aires it so happens, working for the US consulate...

chapters.title: Ellensburg to Beverly Dunes
chapters.text:
This one was brutal.  Beautiful still.  An easy enough ride but hot and dry with no pitstops on the way.  There was scant information about the campsite that I was heading to - Beverly Dunes.  No reviews or pictures, just a blip on the map.  But it was the only place in the vicinity where I was going to end up at the end of the day.

Sweeping vistas, colourful scrub and grasses.  Harsh and washed out in the mid day sun but soft and magical during the early and late hours.  I was heading ultimately to the Gorge Amphitheater for a music festival.  Photos of the amphitheatre look amazing - a really unique setting.  I had no idea it was in such a desert.  

The Colombia River was a sight to behold when I found it.  Looking at it didn't cool me down though.  I was hoping to find a convenience store on the other side of Beverly Bridge but couldn't find one.  Nothing on the map.  Just a small immigrant working community.  No easy way to access the river.  Hoping for the best I continued on to the campground.  I had a water filter with me, I just needed a source of water.  

By the time I got to the campsite I was cooked.  Greeted by a dust tornado I found a bit of shade.  Must've been over 40 degrees.  Set up my tent and crawled into it to escape the heat.  I think I actually started to suffer heat stroke.  Realising I could die there if I didn't find water, and with the bike load lightened, I got back on the road and headed towards the community.  On the way I found a body of water to swim in.  Maybe it was the dregs of the irrigation system, carrying with it all of the fertilisers and runoffs.  It didn't matter, it was that or perish.  Friend of the frogs and the dragonflies, that was the best swim I've ever had.  

I continued to ride after that and found that there was a convenience store right near the base of the bridge.  How about that.  Hydration and beer sorted.  Back to the campsite.  Maybe the most dangerous day that I had throughout the trip, but I was rewarded by the change of light over the dunes as the sun went down.  Incredible...

photos.desc: A defiantly independent American.  Get out of my ways I says.
For somewhere as dry as this, the vegetation can still be full of colour and softness <3

Some abandoned tunnel.  The map said do not pass.  I now know why.  When you exit the tunnel the trail is swamped with mud and overgrown vegetation.  Difficult to traverse.  Would not recommend.  2/5.

This was fun.  A long descent.  Sweeping views of this ancient landscape.  Probably carved out by glaciers or natural forces of some description.  Unless somebody just designed it like this.  Kudos if they did.
Approaching Beverly Dunes.  Beverly Bridge on the left yonder.
Surthriving or absorbing industrial pesticides?  It's all part of modern life.

chapters.title: Beverly Dunes to Ancient Lakes
chapters.text:
Nothing too special to write about this section.  I rode to George.  It's a town near the Gorge Amphitheater.  Guess I was quietly stressed and self distracting about how things were going go when I got to the festival.  Doubting whether riding a bicycle there was a good idea to begin with.  It wasn't really.  But the stupid idea got me out of the house I guess.

Not a terrible ride.  Straight lines and agriculture.  Corn and sprinklers.

The night before the festival I rode out to what I knew to be a natural feature marked on the map called The Ancient Lakes.  With a name like that, how could you not?  Getting there I followed the RideWithGPS map again and I think I was the first person to do that in a long time.  What do you call bush bashing on bike?

Funny story, I got there and it was the night before Independence Day.  All the best spots were taken by non-white people.  ICE would have had a field day.

Not for me though.  I was legal as an eagle.  Same with this other dude.  Born & bred American.  He rocks up late in the piece, takes the last feasible spot in the area right near me as the sun is setting.  It's getting windy.  He's got a 4b4 and all the gear and is attempting to erect a makeshift castle in defiance of the elements as the night closes in.  Is unable to conquer the elements, gets mad that he is unable to provide shelter for his family, yells at his wife, packs up and leaves!

Speculating here but the story goes - he goes home, votes for Trump, applauds the roundup of the immigrants that are the backbone of the economy that are working all around him, then continues to live in misery.  

IDK maybe maybe not.  It was a weird place to camp in.  Especially after the ordeal it took to get there and the whiplash ahead of me.  The geography was amazing.  Ancient Lakes.  I'm no Geologist but this whole side of the Cascades appeared to me to be the dregs of ancient glacial erosion and the remaining landscape now sits in a deathly rain shadow, unloved by God's moistness so enjoyed by the other side of the state but a few kilometres away.  Enjoy God's moistness while you can folks coz there's more of this to come.  Desolate beauty but withholding in that sweet hydration that we've all evolved to know and love.
